title: Bend It Like Beckham
full_review:
An athletic teen Londoner pursues her dream of playing soccer against the wishes of her traditional Sikh parents in the winning clash-of-cultures comedy, "Bend It Like Beckham" (Fox Searchlight).

With daughter Pinky (Archie Panjabi) about to be married to a handsome Indian man, Mrs. Bhamra (Shaheen Khan) is excitedly engulfed in the wedding preparations. But she's not too busy to scold younger daughter Jess (Parminder Nagra) for playing soccer in the park with the boys. Jess has zero interest in staying home to learn Indian cooking when she can be kicking a ball like British soccer hero David Beckham, whose posters adorn her bedroom. In fact, she jumps at the chance when Juliet (Keira Knightley, a near-twin for Winona Ryder) approaches her to join an amateur girl's team coached by an Irish lad, Joe (Jonathan Rhys Meyers), whose knee injury ended his shot at a pro soccer career.

Knowing both her mother and father (Anupam Kher) would disapprove, Jess sneaks out to practice and play with the team. She and tomboy Juliet become best of friends, which in a somewhat contrived subplot, Juliet's mom (Juliet Stevenson) mistakes for a romantic relationship. Their friendship faces a greater obstacle with each of them attracted to Joe.

Another gender-based mistake is made which leads to her sister's engagement being terminated, and an upset Pinky rats on her soccer-playing sibling. Ordered to forget about sports, Jess is caught between respecting her parents' wishes and the urgings of Joe and Juliet to develop her talent.

As co-written and directed by Gurinder Chadha, the genial sports comedy shows lots of heart as it zips through the assorted romantic complications of its sympathetic characters. Some are drawn in broad stereotypes but do gradually get fleshed out, which lifts the film above mere sitcom territory. Making a memorable debut, newcomer Nagra navigates her way through first love, stirrings of independence, fractured friendships and parental confrontations with credible emotional range that bodes well for her career.

The movie has an exuberant tone, especially in the final half-hour as the filmmaker crosscuts between a madly colorful wedding reception and a crucial soccer game, suggesting how the gift of life is to be celebrated and not squandered.

It's curious how both Jess and Juliet's fathers are more supportive of their daughters while their mothers are much more anxious to see them latch onto boyfriends.

Never stooping to mean-spirited characterizations, the narrative bracingly endorses themes of family and friendship, tolerance and teamwork. One may find all the cross-cultural clashes are resolved a bit too neatly at the end but the story builds up good will all along to earn its feel-good finish.

As such, the movie deftly blends comedy, drama, sports action and tentative romance for a sweet-natured coming-of-age tale with underpinnings of girl power.

Because of a discreet sexual situation and references, fleeting drunkenness, minimal profanity and a crass expression, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
